text: A path in a binary tree is a chain of nodes where each pair next to each other has an edge. A node shows up at most once, and the path doesn't have to go through the root. Given the root, return the maximum path sum of any non-empty path.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a path can start and end at any two nodes. It can go up and then come back down, but it can't split into a fork. The sum is just the sum of the node values on it. And it must have at least one node, so I can't return zero for an empty path. Is that right?
Yes. At least one node, no forks.
Got it. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The tree has one to three times ten to the fourth nodes, and each value is between minus one thousand and one thousand.

OK. Two things jump out. Values can be negative, so the tree could be all negative, and then the best path is just the single biggest node. And the tree isn't promised to be balanced, so the depth could be thirty thousand. The key fact: every path has exactly one highest node. I'll call it the bend. From the bend, the path goes down the left side, the right side, or both. So if I try every node as the bend and take the best way down on each side, I cover every path. Quick check on example two: minus ten, nine, twenty, null, null, fifteen, seven. The best path is fifteen, twenty, seven — forty-two. Its bend is twenty, and it never touches the root; going through the root gives only thirty-four, because minus ten costs too much. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would take every pair of nodes, find the path between them through their common ancestor, and add it up. That's n squared pairs, and each path can be long — too slow for thirty thousand nodes. But it's a great checker, and I'll use it later to test my code. This problem reminds me of post-order tree DP, the longest-path-in-a-tree pattern. Each node gets answers from its children, updates a global best with itself as the bend, and returns a single arm to its parent. The only change is that we add up values instead of counting edges, and values can be negative.

Here's the plan. One: path of a node is the best sum going straight down from it; null gives zero. Two: clamp each child's result at zero to drop a losing arm. Three: update the answer with the node as the bend, using both arms, but return the node plus only the larger arm. One thing worth flagging — those two numbers are different, and mixing them up is the classic bug: if I returned both arms, the parent would add itself on top, and the path would fork. And the answer starts at int min, not zero, or an all-negative tree would wrongly get zero. One trade-off: recursion depth is the tree height. An iterative post-order avoids that but is easier to get wrong, so I'll write the recursive one and check the stack later. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The helper follows the plan line by line. Both children are fully done before I touch the answer, so it's a true post-order, and the return value from the root call is thrown away — I only need the answer. One thing worth flagging — the answer is a local in max path sum, passed down by reference, not a class member. That matters if the same Solution object is used twice. With a member that's never reset, calling on minus one and then minus two gives minus one the second time, because the old best is still there. The right answer is minus two. The local version has no state to leak.

Let's dry-run the code on example two. I expect forty-two. The row that matters is twenty. As the bend it uses both arms, twenty plus fifteen plus seven, so the answer becomes forty-two. But it returns only thirty-five: the seven is dropped, because the root can go down only one side. At the root, the best bend is thirty-four, which loses. Output forty-two. Correct. Corner cases: a single minus three returns minus three, thanks to the int min start. All negative, minus one, minus two, minus three: the clamp drops both arms, so the root alone gives minus one. Two with a minus one child: the bad arm is clamped, answer two. And from the slip table: returning both arms turns one, minus one, null, one, one into a fork worth two; the real best is one. The brute-force checker agrees on every tree up to seven nodes.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: counting null children, it's exactly two n plus one calls, each doing constant work. Space is O of h for the recursion stack — a balanced tree of thirty thousand nodes is only fifteen deep. In the worst case the tree is a chain, thirty thousand deep. Without optimization each frame is about ninety-six bytes, and on an eight megabyte stack the crash depth is about eighty-seven thousand — a two point nine times margin. Fine, but not huge: an AddressSanitizer build does overflow on the longest chain. If stack is a concern, I'd switch to an iterative post-order. Oh, one more thing — overflow. The biggest possible path is every node at one thousand: thirty million, about seventy-one times below int max. And int min is only compared, never added to. So int is safe.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed every path by its single highest node, and kept the two numbers apart: both arms for the answer, one arm for the return, with a small case showing what a fork does. You explained the negatives carefully: the clamp drops a losing arm, and starting at int min instead of zero keeps a single minus one correct. And you checked the limits yourself: a local answer so repeated calls are safe, int is enough, and only a two point nine times stack margin, with an iterative fallback. Good work.
